name: Pol Pot

meta.summary: After capturing Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975, the Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot established Democratic Kampuchea and abolished money, markets, private property, schools, courts, and religion, forcibly emptying the cities into rural labor communes. The regime carried out systematic execution, torture, forced labor, and starvation, with credible estimates of roughly 1.5-2 million or more deaths, including targeted killing of Cham Muslims, ethnic Vietnamese and Chinese, Buddhist monks, and former officials. A Vietnamese invasion overthrew the regime in January 1979.

editor_note: The regime near-totally captured every domain, so all six 'condition' extremes fire with high confidence. Death-toll-dependent and total-blackout claims are flagged medium confidence per matching discipline.

scored_actions.note: The Khmer Rouge abolished the courts and the formal legal system; 'justice' was administered by Angkar and the security apparatus with no independent judicial review.
No competitive national election existed; Pol Pot and the covert Communist Party of Kampuchea held power via military victory, never subject to a contested vote.
The single 20 March 1976 election for the Kampuchean People's Representative Assembly had all candidates hand-picked by the CPK, voting limited to the 'politically reliable' and supervised by cadre.
All mass media and information were state-controlled; the regime abolished communications and sealed the country off, leaving only official propaganda.
The regime abolished postal service and communication and cut Cambodia off from outside contact, imposing a near-total information blackout.
Movement, assembly, and daily life were fully controlled; the population was forced into communal work brigades, and travel required permission.
Mass detention of civilians without trial in a nationwide network of security centers; roughly 14,000-20,000 people passed through S-21 (Tuol Sleng) alone, of whom only a handful survived.
Any perceived dissent, connection to the former Khmer Republic, or 'new people' status was treated as a capital offense against Angkar, criminalizing broad categories of the population.
No institution constrained the executive; the Representative Assembly was a rubber-stamp body that rarely met, and real power rested with the secret CPK standing committee under Pol Pot.
The CPK/Angkar governed by directive without legislative check, issuing sweeping orders (mass evacuation, abolition of money) with no lawmaking process.

The state routinely imprisoned and executed for political reasons; the Yale program estimates roughly 1.7 million deaths (about 21% of the population) from execution, forced labor, starvation, and disease.

Systematic violence targeted ethnic and religious groups: an estimated ~500,000 Cham Muslims, ethnic Vietnamese and Chinese, and Buddhist monks (over half killed); a Khmer Rouge order declared 'The Cham nation no longer exists.'

sources.title: The question of genocide and Cambodia's Muslims

scored_actions.note: Mass extrajudicial killings at the 'killing fields' and forced disappearances of detainees; senior Lon Nol officials and officers were executed within days of the April 1975 takeover.
Head of state Prince Norodom Sihanouk was forced to resign on 5 April 1976 and held under house arrest; the regime also purged and imprisoned its own cadres accused of treason.
Torture was systematic in state detention; at S-21 prisoners were tortured to extract forced confessions before execution.
Ethnic Vietnamese were expelled from the country and the regime ordered the abolition of Cham nationality, language, and religion.

wins: Emptied Phnom Penh and all cities on day one (17 April 1975), atomizing any urban base for organized opposition.
Executed the former Lon Nol leadership and officer corps within days, foreclosing a counter-revolution.
Built a pervasive secret security apparatus (Angkar, S-21, zone prisons) that enforced total control through terror.
Sealed the country from outside contact, delaying international scrutiny for years.
failures: Abolishing money and markets and forcing agrarian collectivization triggered mass famine that destroyed the regime's own labor base.
Killing doctors, teachers, engineers, and technicians gutted state and economic capacity.
Paranoid internal purges (notably the Eastern Zone) hollowed out the party and army and pushed cadres to defect to Vietnam.
Border raids provoked Vietnam's December 1978 invasion, which toppled the regime within weeks by 7 January 1979.
